## Visual tests are allowed again (2026-09-12, #924)

The standing "NO VISUAL TESTS" clause that the #904-#923 tasks carried (do not
run `run_examples.sh`, `make test-examples`, a screenshot gate or an example in
a window; hand the visual check to the user) is LIFTED. From #924 on, a queue
task may run the visual example gates and examples itself to verify its own
claims — with explicit timeouts, one run at a time, and still never alongside a
live `watch-tests.sh` run. Every still-open task that carried the clause has it
replaced by a "VISUAL TESTS OK" note; the clause stays verbatim on the closed
tasks as the record of how they were verified.

## How SUMU reads this file

SUMU owns the list between the markers below and rebuilds it on every save.
Anything worth keeping goes above the start marker.

SUMU writes `[queued]` and `[>claude]` / `[>codex]`. The agent writes the
outcome, in the same commit as the work: `[x]` done, `[postponed]`, or
`[failed]` / `[question]` — both stop the queue, with the question after
`QUESTION:` in the line body.
Never put the task you are running back to `[ ]` when you stop it. An earlier
`[postponed]` task whose blocker is gone is reopened by changing its own line
back to `[ ]` (keep its `#id`), never by copying it into a new task.

File a new task as `- [ ] the task text`; SUMU mints the `#id`, so never
guess one. Line order is the queue order.

A task may name the model it runs on with a group near the head of its text,
after any leading `[tag]`: `- [ ] [a tag] {model:gpt-6-astra} the task text`.
The model picks the agent too (`gpt-6-astra`, `gpt-5.6-sol` run on Codex;
`claude-opus-5-5`, `claude-fable-5-1` and the like on Claude); a task with no
group runs on the chat's current model. `{difficulty:N}` is no longer read
(since 2026-11-02): do not write it; old lines keep it until SUMU rewrites them.
Split large tasks without lowering their model requirement. Completed task
levels remain historical records; a checked task is not proof of visual approval.

(`lib/treeGen/`, not based on any existing tree code), that matches

and waits for a score (`[question]`). The tasks that were
open before are in `ASTRA_TREE_QUEUE_BACKUP.md` (a backup, not a queue).
The landscape plan below is on hold with them.

## Landscape art plan: Autumn Grove and Huge Forest

The landscape tasks below implement the future-plans section of the local
reference study, `references/study.html` in the looks-development repository
(moved there from peli_ideoita on 2026-10-26: looks-development is the private,
Git LFS repository of every iteration's pictures and videos).
Its `crops/`, contact sheets and `manifest.json` give stable references:
T01-T10 trees/trunks, R01-R07 rocks, C01-C03 clouds, G01-G03 ground cover.
Read the images, not only their captions. Keep these private reference images
outside the repository; make original production assets and record their source
or creation method. If the study is unavailable, report that before making a
style decision from memory.

- **Art target:** the current collection is below the desired quality. Birch is
  the closest starting point, not a finished benchmark. Replace the angular,
  individual-leaf look with coherent foliage masses and delicate textured edges;
  do not replace it with visibly separate balls or flat sheets. Grass needs a
  full overhaul. Improve existing species before adding more tree varieties.
- **Ownership and scope:** shared generators, materials and placement live in
  `lib/`; scene composition and tuning live in the examples. Rae owns generation,
  ECS data, configuration and resource lifetime; WGSL handles GPU work. No new
  renderer policy in C, copied example shaders, per-leaf entities or per-tree
  texture allocations. Reuse the shipped instancing, surface-image and ownership
  paths. A new language feature is outside this series.
- **Species:** every existing tree gets a real species identity and visual
  reference. Colors are seasonal/cultivar variants, not automatically different
  species. The inventory task resolves the unnamed entries before their visual
  tasks run and updates those task titles without changing assigned queue IDs.
  Preserve successful narrow cypresses, normal-sized spruces and the single
  mature camphor. Trunks remain rigid: do not reintroduce whole-tree wobble.
- **Recovery review (2026-10-25):** the first landscape
  implementation series was rejected. Its commits are preserved on
  `recovery/landscape-before-review-20261025`. Birch, grass and flower visuals
  are not approved foundations for other species. Review the matched recovery
  comparisons before continuing any dependent art task. Do not call a technique
  proven or a species finished because geometry tests or nonblank frames pass.
  The eight rejected attempts are superseded `[postponed]` records; resume with
  the six `[ ]` recovery tasks, starting at #64669660. Do not rerun both versions.
- **Visual acceptance:** save and inspect matched before/after views with fixed
  camera, seed, sun, exposure and resolution; include close, medium, side,
  below-canopy and backlit views where relevant. Check motion with an orbit and
  a walking camera, plus day/night response. Compare to the named reference
  crops. Explain remaining mismatches; a regenerated screenshot or green gate
  alone does not establish that the style is good. Never claim
  approval that has not been given.
- **Integration:** 138 is the close-up showcase; 143 is the large, traversable
  forest. Shared tree/grass/rock changes also reach 136 and 137 in the same task;
  preserve the forward/deferred, shadow and atlas paths. Retain working existing
  LODs and bounds, but do not turn a species task into a new billboard project.
  Use existing knobs for comparisons, and remove obsolete experiments after
  choosing a result rather than accumulating rendering modes.
- **Verification:** follow AGENTS.md's narrow-test matrix, use explicit timeouts
  for every build/test/example, and run visual examples one at a time. Generator
  changes need deterministic geometry/valid-index/bounds checks; material, wind
  or card changes need the relevant hardware checks as well as affected example
  gates. Format changed Rae, run the example-copy gate and bump the patch version
  for lib changes. Full-suite-required changes run `compiler/tools/watch-tests.sh`;
  otherwise reserve the series-wide suite for the final validation task. Record
  timings under comparable load; do not promise a frame budget from a busy run.

- [x] #55147248 [box3d/ecs: a kinematic body overshoots its pose when a frame runs several steps] Found by game proto2 (2026-11-17): under load (several of its headless checks at once) a walker walked through a kinematic box, which was flying about at 400 m/s, far from its Transform3D. box3d/ecs/PhysicsSystems.physicsPushSystem calls b3Body_SetTargetTransform (the velocity to reach the pose in one fixed step) only when the Transform3D's stamp changed, so only on the first step of a frame; the body keeps that velocity on the frame's other steps, overshoots, gets a bigger correction the next frame, and at 3 or more steps a frame the swing grows to the world's top speed. At one step a frame (60 fps, unloaded) it never shows. Fix in the push: remember a kinematic body's target, and on each step where it got no new pose, aim it at that target again (or zero its velocity once there), so a kinematic body written once a frame stops at its pose. Check: a case that writes a kinematic box's pose once and steps 4 times, the box at its pose with zero velocity after; one that moves it each frame of 3 steps and stays within a step's move of it. Game proto2 works round it by touching every kinematic Transform3D before each step; it removes that after the release. Done 2026-11-17 in Rae 0.4.2 (tagged here, NOT pushed: push for game proto2 to pin it and drop its workaround): RigidBody keeps a kinematic body's last pushed pose (`target`, `aimed`); physicsPushSystem, on a step with no new pose, aims the body at it again (b3Body_SetTargetTransform, not waking it) and, once it is there, zeroes its velocities and stops aiming. Case 1515_box3d_kinematic_steps: written once and stepped 4 times it stays at x 1 with no velocity (the old code went 1 2 3 4); moved every frame of 3 steps it stays at its pose. Case 999_box3d_ecs_determinism's expected output changed where its kinematic platform carries a box (entity 11 and one contact fewer; still identical across worker counts): the platform no longer overshoots on a frame's second step. Checked: the 24 box3d/ecs cases; the 123 and 125 gates (123 still equal to playground.golden).

- [x] #90944914 [compiler/ownership] {difficulty:4} Reusing a heap-owning struct in two List literals aliases its nested buffers and double-frees at scope exit. Confirmed under ASan on 0.2.125: `type Payload { items: List(Int) }`; `makePayload()` returns a Payload with `{ 1, 2, 3 }`; `let payload: Payload = makePayload(); let first: List(Payload) = { payload }; let second: List(Payload) = { payload }; log("{first.length} {second.length}")`. Both insertions emit plain struct copies; generated cleanup drops both lists. The same failure occurs with the second insertion through `List.add(value: payload)`. Preserve ordinary deep-copy semantics unless `own` is explicit; cover nested-list independence, repeated insertion, mutation and exact cleanup with ASan/UBSan. Found while checking textured birch impostors; that hardware test constructs a fresh subject per owner as a workaround. — DONE (0.2.128). Literal path: a list-literal element that is a place (local, field, index) of a heap-owning type is now deep-copied (c_stmt.c emit_collection_element, used by both literal lowerings); `own x` moves; fresh values move as before. List.add path: sema never ran the own-argument check for the backend-bound generic List methods (no decl_link), so the second add of a moved local was accepted; now it finds the declaration by name and receiver type, and the second add is the `use of moved value` error (docs/ownership-model.md rule; a deep copy needs `"{x}"` or a copy binding). Flow fixes so the check holds: a move on a path that returns does not reach later code, a `loop let x in` binding is fresh each pass. Fixed the use-after-moves it found: lib/physics ShapeProxy, WorldBodies, WorldShapes, Sensors (read fields before set), lib/ui/SceneImports, lib/app3d/GltfLevel, example 99 (copies), cases 415 and 554. New cases 1236 (copies: nested lists, repeated insertion, mutation, Strings, fields, view returns, own), 1237 (second add is the error), 1238 (returning-branch move); 1236 and 1238 run in compiler/tools/asan-check.sh under ASan+UBSan. Full suite 899/899.

- [x] #96933372 The tests take rougly 26 minutes. We have roughly 10 tasks in the QUEUE.md if each one ends with a test suite run, we take a huge amount of time only on tests. - Figure out if tests can be run faster? More parallel? Are they running in parallel? - Does every QUEUE.md task need to run the whole test suite? What could we do? You may write into the tasks new instructions on when to run tests, or just make them faster or whatever you see fit to fix this issue, or make it better. — DONE: a full run now takes 308 s (5.1 min), down from 27.5 min; same verdicts (829 passed, 0 failed). Every run now prints each stage's time and the 15 slowest cases, which showed four causes, all fixed. (1) run_tests.sh <name> walked all 843 case directories (two forks each) to find the one case; the parallel runner calls it once per case, so a tiny case cost ~5 s. It now looks only at the directories the name can match (unit cases 1219 s -> 131 s). (2) Every case compiled the whole C runtime (1.7 s of a small case's 1.9 s C build). The compiler now keeps the runtime object in ~/.cache/rae/runtime/, keyed by the compile command and the runtime sources (compiler/src/runtime_cache.c); this also makes every rae run faster (version 0.2.93). (3) The wasm smoke gate waited the full 60 s timeout for each of two headless Chrome pages, which print their result after ~1 s; Chrome is now stopped at the result line (150 s -> 32 s). (4) tsan-check ran 25 TSan programs one after another; they now run in parallel, with the runtime built under TSan once (157 s -> 58 s; a RAE_TSAN_FILTER=106_mobile_ui run no longer fails on a missing fixture). (1) The devtools tailer (tools/devtools-web/src/server/testLogTailer.ts) saw a new run only when the log got SHORTER; when the run before was short (an agent's one-case run, ~600 bytes) the full run grew past that size between two polls, the tailer read on from the old offset and missed @@RAE_RUN_START, took the run for an un-instrumented one and ended it at every silence over 6 s: the slow pre-suite checks became a string of 6-10 s runs, and the clock looked normal once the unit cases streamed. It now compares the file's first line (the marker, with its run id) every poll. (3) A devtools restart during a run (the dev runner restarts it on every src/ change) started reading at the end of the log and lost the run: the tailer now attaches to a marked run that has not ended, and a marked run's clock starts at the epoch in its marker. New tools/devtools-web/scripts/testLogTailerCheck.ts reproduces (1) and (3) against the old tailer (5 failed) and passes now; the lock was checked with a stand-in make (waits, gives up after the limit, runs once the first ends, clears dead and reused-pid locks); tsc --noEmit clean. - [x] #23474178 {difficulty:4} One GPU timing module, not two. lib/GpuTiming.rae (#528, 289 lines) and lib/gpu/GpuTiming.rae (#871, 430 lines) both declare `type GpuTiming` and do the same job, per-pass GPU timestamps: the old one maps its readback buffer and WAITS for the GPU each frame, and writes profiler counters (gpu.<pass>, gpu.total) for a Perfetto capture; the new one never waits (manager-owned buffers and ReadbackId through gpu/GpuResources and gpu/GpuLifetime, an `available` fallback when the adapter has no timestamp queries) and is what the renderer (lib/RendererPassTiming, RAE_GPU_PASS_TIMING) and the water (lib/water/WaterSystem, WaterGpuBridge, WaterPerf) use. Nothing in lib/ or examples/ imports the old one any more; only the hardware check checks/gpuTiming does. Two modules named GpuTiming also make `GpuTiming.x` ambiguous when both are loaded (case 725), and, while type names are program-wide, no program can load both. Do: keep lib/gpu/GpuTiming as the only one; add to it what only the old one has, the profiler counters: an optional step that publishes the last completed sample's per-pass times as Profiler counters under the pass names (a frame or two late is fine for a capture), and the pass names where the caller gives them; move checks/gpuTiming onto it (or fold it into checks/gpuManagerTiming); delete lib/GpuTiming.rae; update docs/water-performance.md and docs/webgpu-readback.md, which name GpuTiming.collect as the blocking capture tool (Context.webgpuMapRead stays as the blocking readback diagnostic). Check: a profiler capture (Profile.maybeAutoStart) of a walker example still shows gpu.<pass> counters; RAE_GPU_PASS_TIMING=1 lines unchanged in 136 and 141; checks/run.sh gpuManagerTiming and the moved gpuTiming check pass on hardware; the suite passes. VISUAL TESTS OK. — DONE: lib/gpu/GpuTiming is the only GPU timing module; lib/GpuTiming.rae and checks/gpuTiming are deleted. It gained what only the old one had: pass names (timedPassNamed; timedPass names a pass pass<index>; recordTimingMark takes the name of the span it starts), the last completed sample (lastNames, lastMicroseconds, kept by collectTiming and collectTimingMarks) and publishTimingCounters(timing, profiler), which writes gpu.<name> per pass and gpu.total into a capture (a frame or a few late; nothing outside a capture). The renderer (RendererPassTiming) names its marks after the graph passes, runs under RAE_PROFILE as well as RAE_GPU_PASS_TIMING=1 (the [gpu passes] log only under the latter), and publishGpuPassCounters(renderer, profiler) publishes them; the walker calls it each frame. WaterPerf names its pass after its label (gpu.fft / gpu.surface). checks/gpuTiming folded into checks/gpuManagerTiming, which now names a pass and checks the published counters; it also requests the device features before the bootstrap (chooseDeviceFeatures), so it times real passes instead of always taking the no-timestamps fallback. Docs updated (water-performance, webgpu-readback, gpu-resource-identity-design, unsafe-boundary, webgpu-c-surface-audit, checks/README). Checked: a RAE_PROFILE capture of 136 has gpu.<pass> counters (340 samples each); RAE_GPU_PASS_TIMING=1 lines unchanged in 136 and 141; checks/run.sh 9 passed (gpuManagerTiming: 5 frames timed, counters gpu.pass0 gpu.heavy gpu.total); RAE_WATER_PERF still logs; gates 136 and 141 pass; full suite 826 passed, 0 failed. VERSION 0.2.90.
- [x] #58125876 What is this? Needs fixing? Duplicate function? : - `makeDir`: lib/ui/WindowGeometry now calls Filesystem.makeDir, which also creates missing parent folders. The prelude's Sys.makeDir makes only one folder, and the window-geometry path is nested. — ANSWER: yes, it was a duplicate, and a trap: lib had two `makeDir(path: view String) ret Bool` with the same name and parameters but different behavior. Sys.makeDir (the prelude, plain POSIX mkdir) made ONE folder; Filesystem.makeDir (SDL_CreateDirectory, SDL builds only) also made the missing parents. Which one a bare `makeDir` meant depended on what the file opened, and the new ambiguity error (0.2.98) caught WindowGeometry, which opens Filesystem and needs the nested `.rae/apps/<app>` folder; I had only qualified that call. FIXED (compiler 0.2.100): now there is one: Sys.makeDir makes every missing folder on the way, like `mkdir -p`, written in Rae over the existing one-call shim (rae_sys_make_dir, which already counts an existing folder as success); Filesystem.makeDir, its extern and rae_ext_Filesystem_makeDir in runtime_image_sdl3.c are deleted; WindowGeometry and Filesystem.renderPath call it bare. Existing one-level callers (HotReload, 106's AppCache, cases 544, 941, 1036) work unchanged. Checked: a scratch program (nested absolute path, again, relative nested path, empty path false), emit-c of all 106 programs, full suite 848 passed 0 failed, 136's example gate passed; docs/filesystem-and-paths.md updated.

The plan is to port simple reference servers to Rae and measure them against the same servers in Rust and JavaScript (Node, and possibly Bun). I'm new to the server area, so explain web-server specifics briefly when they matter for a decision. You have room to design this yourself. Follow our usual flow: investigate → write up a design with the forks surfaced → I decide → implement. Don't implement before I approve the design. Reference material (read it, don't treat it as gospel) - hashrocket/websocket-shootout: tiny WebSocket protocol with two messages, `echo` and `broadcast`, plus its Go load tool `websocket-bench`. It dates from 2016, so its Rust and JS servers use outdated libraries. - sharkbench/sharkbench: HTTP + JSON + I/O benchmark, one folder per implementation, runs limited to 1 core via Docker. - the-benchmarker/web-frameworks: mid-size, per-framework config.yaml. - TechEmpower FrameworkBenchmarks: too big to use, but its test-type definitions (plaintext, json, …) are the de facto standard spec. - Load generators: oha / wrk / bombardier for HTTP, websocket-bench for WebSocket. Suggested phasing (adjust if you see a better order) 1. HTTP/1.1 `GET /plaintext` and `GET /json`, TechEmpower-compatible semantics. 2. WebSocket echo + broadcast, compatible with the websocket-shootout protocol. 3. Game-style variant: N clients in a room, server broadcasts state at a fixed tick (e.g. 30 Hz). Measure tick jitter and fan-out cost, not just req/s. TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are out of scope for now. The most important part of the design: what lives where Classify every piece of the suite into one of these buckets, and justify it in the design doc: A. Committed to the rae repo Likely candidates: - the Rae server implementations - our own short written spec for each benchmark, so we aren't bound to an external repo's drift - runner and fetch scripts - a pinned manifest of external sources (repo URL + commit SHA) - a correctness checker that validates responses before any timing runs Decide where this lives (e.g. a top-level `bench/` vs under `examples/`), following the repo's existing conventions and module naming rules (folders camelCase, files PascalCase). B. External, fetched not vendored Cloned reference repos and load-generator tools, pulled by a script at pinned SHAs into a gitignored directory. Decide whether we use the external Rust/JS reference servers as-is, or write and commit our own small, modern Rust/JS references (e.g. tokio/hyper or axum, Node `http`/`ws`, uWebSockets.js). Note that the shootout's are outdated. If any external code gets copied into the repo, check its license and keep attribution. C. Generated, never committed Build outputs, raw result files (JSON/CSV), charts and reports, all produced by scripts. Decide whether anything derived is committed (e.g. a dated summary table in docs as a baseline), or whether results stay entirely local or in CI artifacts. Also decide - How runs stay fair: same machine, warmup, multiple runs, core pinning or limits, and which metrics (req/s, p50/p99 latency, RSS memory, and for phase 3 tick jitter). I'm on macOS, so Docker-based CPU limits may not apply; propose what's realistic. - How it's invoked: e.g. a `make bench-servers` target. It must NOT run as part of `make test-examples` or normal tests; only the correctness checker might belong there. - Dependencies: what the user must install (Go for websocket-bench, Rust toolchain, Node, oha, …), and how scripts detect missing ones and fail clearly. Rae-specific - First find out what Rae can do today for networking: sockets, an event loop / non-blocking I/O, threads, FFI to libc or kqueue. A server benchmark is meaningless if we bolt on hacks. - List language or stdlib gaps as separate proposed tickets with difficulty estimates, rather than working around them. Respect the language design rules: no escape hatches, and view/mod can't be stored in structs. That last rule will shape how connection state is held, so address it explicitly. - Check real syntax in the repo before writing any Rae code in the doc. Deliverable for this round A design doc (e.g. docs/server-benchmarks-design.md) containing: - the directory layout with the A/B/C classification above - the per-benchmark spec - the reference-implementation choice - the runner design - the Rae capability gap list - a numbered list of design forks for me to decide Keep it concise. No implementation yet. ``` I left out an actual design so the agent does that part. Layout: benchmarks/servers/ following benchmarks/list_access (per-language folders, run.sh, gitignored build/, committed results/) with our own specs, Rae servers, own Rust (hyper/tokio-tungstenite) + Node (http/ws) + Bun references with lockfiles, check.sh, fetch.sh + external.lock pinning externals into ~/.cache/rae/servers. It passed alone twice right after, and in the next full run. The fixture runs Box3D's own scheduler threads (workerCount = the pool's) while 10 test jobs compete for the CPU. Find out what produced no output (per-case timeout under load? a crash or deadlock in the threaded step, e.g. oversubscription?): reproduce by running it many times under parallel load (e.g. 20 copies at once), check the runner's timeout handling for this case, and either fix the cause or give the case a worker count/timeout that cannot starve. — Done (2026-10-06). Found a real race, plus a diagnostics gap; the exact empty-output symptom did not reproduce. (1) Not the program: the fixture binary ran 2,000 times (20 copies at once, 100 rounds, under a full CPU hog on every core) without one failure, crash or hang; the runner has no per-case timeout, so a hang would have stalled the suite, not emptied the output. (2) The race was in `rae run`, which the runner calls for every case. 20 concurrent rae runs of 999 plus the other Box3D fixtures failed 1 run in 100 with 'unknown type name rae_String'. Cause: run_compiled_file wrote $TMPDIR/rae_compiled_<pid>.c (pid-unique), but build_c_backend_output copies the runtime sources and headers next to the C file, i.e. into the SHARED $TMPDIR, and the C includes "rae_runtime.h" from its own directory, so concurrent runs rewrote the one header while gcc read it. Fix (compiler/src/main.c): each rae run builds in a private mkdtemp scratch dir (C, binary, runtime copies), removed on every exit path. After: 300 concurrent runs with 0 failures; no scratch dirs left; idle-wakeups.sh and the parallel-safety notes (run_tests_parallel.sh, docs/parallel-tests.md) corrected. (3) Diagnostics: a failing compiled run case now prints the program's exit code, or 'none - the driver stopped before running it', and for an empty output the last raw lines the comparison normally filters (@@ lines included), so a recurrence explains itself. The suite's blank result still has no confirmed cause: a build-race failure prints errors, so this race does not obviously produce a blank, and I could not make one happen. Full suite 658/0. - [x] #10931037 {difficulty:4} [spawn S3c: fork-join over shared data, 8 compute threads] Depends on S3a (landed 0.1.251). Two findings of the S3a measurement (docs/lightweight-spawn-design.md §12): (1) fork-join over data is bound by copying the halves (the 16 M sum stays 0.06x of sequential: one copy costs more than the whole sum), so tasks inside a taskScope need to read data owned outside it through a `view` (§3.1's open point; today a view argument makes the spawn sequential). That is a language rule: write the proposal into the design doc and ask before implementing. (2) The waiting main thread is not a worker, so 7 of 8 threads compute: let a waiting off-pool thread help (or count it in the pool) and measure the near-linear fork-join target on 8 cores with only a leaf-size cut-off. — PART (2) DONE (0.1.253, docs/lightweight-spawn-design.md §14.1): a waiting off-pool thread (main) now helps like a worker (depth cap 32), so 8 threads compute; benchmarks/spawn `work` mode (copy-free fork-join): 6.8-7.1x on 8 cores from 64 to 32 768 leaves, 1.0x on one worker. PART (1) DONE (0.1.254, §14.2, approved as recommended): a spawn inside a taskScope lends a `view` of a local declared before the scope / a parameter / a string literal; the lent local is frozen until the scope ends; the scope keeps a task group and waits for its borrowers at its end and before ret/break/continue (instead of forbidding Tasks to escape, so List(Task) works); `mod` and lending outside a taskScope stay errors. benchmarks/spawn sum, 16 M ints, 8 workers: lent fork-join 1.4-1.9 ms vs copying 31-46 ms, = parallelLoop 1.4 ms (memory-bound). Fixtures 1077 (also TSan), 1078.

- [x] #67388129 {difficulty:4} [language design — atomics and staged parallel work for the physics solver: DESIGN, then [question]] [language design — atomics and staged parallel work for the physics solver: DESIGN, then [question]] docs/physics-performance-plan.md §4-§5 item 3. Box3D's solver keeps every worker inside ONE task across a few hundred stage barriers per step (11 stage kinds; warm start, solve and relax per color, per substep): workers claim fixed-size blocks with a per-block atomic compare-and-swap on a monotonic sync index, count completions with an atomic counter, and spin with a CPU yield until the main thread publishes the next stage in one atomic word (~50 atomic call sites). Re-dispatching a pool task per stage would cost more than the stage, and Rae has no function values, so a library cannot take the block work as a callback. Recommended shape, to write up with a worked example from the contact solver: an `Atomic(Int)` / `Atomic(Int32)` library type over C11 stdatomic (load, store, fetchAdd, compareExchange; never on floats), a `cpuRelax()` intrinsic, and the worker pool's guaranteed-concurrent parallelLoop mode — the solver then runs Box3D's own stage loop, as the C does. Compare it honestly with the alternative, a dedicated stage/barrier construct that hides the atomics. ALSO design here the guaranteed-concurrent mode (every worker running one iteration at once — what spin barriers need; moved here 2026-10-03, since it only serves spin barriers and those need atomics): the design must state (1) its determinism story (identical bits for any worker count, like parallelLoop) and (2) its RAE_WORKERS=1 behavior — one worker cannot have all iterations live at once, so barriers must degrade to sequential stages, never deadlock. Per-worker scratch is NOT part of this: it is chunk scratch (docs/concurrency-model.md §5, fixture 946), and no workerIndex rule is to be added. Until this lands the solver stays sequential and the parallelLoop checker rules stay as they are. List the compiler and runtime work, and end with [question] for a choice; the implementation is a follow-up task. Never @-attributes. The worker pool and parallelLoop have landed. — DESIGNED in docs/parallel-stages-design.md (nothing implemented). Measured first (benchmarks/parallel_stages: a 220-stage solver-shaped step, 32 blocks of ~1.5 us per stage, as one parallelLoop per stage vs one flat parallelLoop): barrier 1.3 / 1.4 / 4.7 us per stage at 2 / 4 / 8 workers — staged 1.85x / 3.38x / 4.33x vs flat 1.96x / 3.79x / 7.6x (Box3D's own C reaches 3.4x at 8 workers on the pyramid). So re-dispatching per stage does NOT cost more than the stage at 4 workers; at 8 the cost is the pool's single shared claim word, a runtime-only fix. Three options written up with determinism, RAE_WORKERS=1 behavior, deadlock risk and compiler/runtime work: C (recommended) a stage is a parallelLoop — no new construct, no atomics, determinism by construction, sequential stages at RAE_WORKERS=1, cannot deadlock; follow-up is a runtime launch-path rewrite (per-worker start offsets, per-chunk claims, inline one-chunk stages, per-worker done flags) accepted when 8-worker barriers are ≤ ~1.5 us. A: Atomic(Int)/Atomic(Int32) + cpuRelax() + a parallelTeam keyword (the guaranteed-concurrent mode) running Box3D's loop line by line — determinism by three unchecked conventions, and it can deadlock (a leader that waits for a helper hangs at RAE_WORKERS=1); progress rule = Box3D's (iteration 0 on the caller can finish every stage alone, helpers only steal). B: a parallelStages construct = C's semantics with workers resident, only worth it if C's runtime fix falls short. Found while writing the worked example: EVERY option needs one more thing — the solver writes body states at indices from constraint data (disjoint only by graph coloring, which the checker cannot prove, and restructuring to own-index writes would break bit-exactness with the oracle). DECIDED 2026-10-03: Option C (a stage is a parallelLoop) with `unsafe` for the coloring's disjoint writes — and IMPLEMENTED: (1) `unsafe { }` in a parallelLoop body lifts the write rule (ret/break/continue stay rejected); every List set/modAt there reports its element to rae_parallel_check_write, and RAE_PARALLEL_CHECK=1 / Parallel.checkWrites(enabled: true) stops the program on two iterations writing one element ('iterations 3 and 5 both wrote parallel[7]'); fixture 947 (greedy coloring of 200 contacts on 64 bodies, one parallelLoop per color, bit-identical to the sequential solve at 1/2/3/8 workers, then a wrong coloring caught). (2) launch path: per-worker contiguous chunk ranges with cache-line-padded claim words and stealing, one completion add per worker per job, one-chunk jobs inline, 250 us clock-based spin before sleeping, lock-free pool-start check; back-to-back launch at 8 workers 3.9 -> 2.0 us. Barrier per stage measured side by side with a Box3D-style C reference of the same step (benchmarks/parallel_stages/c/box3d_style.c, interleaved, machine at load 5-11): 4 workers Rae 1.4-1.7 us vs Box3D-style 0.55-1.3 us, 8 workers Rae 2.2-3.0 us (one 9.4 us outlier) vs 1.65-3.4 us — usually within 1.0-1.4x of Box3D's own scheme; the absolute 1.5 us at 8 workers is out of reach on this loaded machine for both. Side finding: the same block arithmetic is 2x slower in Rae than in C (scalar codegen, not threading). TSan clean at 2 and 8 workers; full suite 599/599. Docs: parallel-stages-design.md §9, concurrency-model.md §5, physics-performance-plan.md item 3. Version 0.1.104.

- [x] #52781647 {difficulty:4} [language design — a 4-wide float type (Float4) for SIMD: DESIGN plus a measured prototype, then [question]] [language design — a 4-wide float type (Float4) for SIMD: DESIGN plus a measured prototype, then [question]] docs/physics-performance-plan.md §2 and §5 item 4: Box3D's NEON build is 1.35-1.5x faster than scalar on contact-heavy scenes (5 050-box pyramid: 8.1 vs 11.8 ms per step single-threaded; 2.75 vs 3.8 ms at 4 workers), 1.1-1.2x on piles, 1.0x on joints — it is the margin that keeps the featured example within 4 ms unless the port is within ~1.05x of C. Design a `Float4` value type (lane-wise arithmetic, load/store from a List(Float), compare/select, horizontal ops) lowering to SSE2 / NEON / wasm SIMD128, with the scalar struct as the fallback. Box3D keeps its SIMD path bit-identical to the scalar one (no approximate rsqrt; convex_manifold.c 'needs to match the SIMD version'), so the Float4 contact solver must stay bit-exact against the scalar oracle. Prototype it on the contact-solver kernel extracted into benchmarks/ (scalar Rae vs Float4 Rae vs C SIMD) and record the numbers. End with [question] for approval of the surface. Needs P4 (the scalar contact solver exists). — DONE (design + prototype): docs/float4-design.md proposes a builtin Float4 (lane fields x y z w, lane-wise + - * /, named functions with scalar-exact semantics: compare-and-select min/max/abs, unfused mulAdd, no approximate rsqrt), a separate Mask4 for comparisons, defined-order horizontal ops, opt-returning load/store from List(Float), lowered to NEON / SSE2 / wasm SIMD128 inline intrinsics with the scalar struct as fallback. Prototype benchmarks/float4_solver (run.sh): the real P4 wide contact solver over a SIMD FloatWide is bit-exact with Box3D's scalar AND NEON builds and with the scalar Rae solver; Float4 is 1.32-1.35x faster than scalar Rae (C NEON vs C scalar: 1.62-1.66x); with a higher inline threshold Rae scalar is 0.96x C scalar and Float4 is within 1.15x of C NEON (load ~8 during the runs; numbers in §5). A native vector type is no faster than a struct with SIMD primitives: the win needs the primitives inline, not a special representation. QUESTION: approve the Float4 surface of docs/float4-design.md §2 (the four questions in §7: separate Mask4 vs masks as Float4; lane-wise operators vs named functions only; opt-returning load vs an Array-indexed form; living in the prelude lib/core)? On approval the compiler work and the FloatWide switch are §8. — ANSWERED 2026-10-04: approved with changes (docs/float4-design.md §0): Mask4 stays separate (select, and/or/not, any/all only); named functions only, no lane-wise operators; the load returns opt Float4; an imported module lib/Float4.rae, not the prelude. Implementation queued as '[compiler — implement Float4 / Mask4 and switch FloatWide over]'.

For a struct whose list elements own heap (lib/physics/dynamics Contact: `manifolds: List(Manifold)`, each Manifold with a points List) the alias drop is empty, so the deep copy copyAtDefault returned leaks: 2 buffers per destroyed contact before the physics code was changed to read contacts through viewAt (2026-10-04, fixture 957). A `let` binding of the same call gets the owning drop. Make statement temporaries of calls that return an owned value (copyAtDefault, any plain `ret T`) use the owning drop, keeping the alias drop only where the callee really returns an alias; add a leak fixture with rae_ext_rae_mem_stats_buf_outstanding. — DONE: only the `view`-argument temporaries were affected (a member read like `.flags` already got the owning drop); both argument sites in c_call.c passed owns_heap only for an object literal. New c_stmt_temp_value_owns: an object literal or a call that returns a value it made is owned; a buffer-get intrinsic or a callee whose body returns an alias (the same scan a `let` uses) keeps the alias drop. Fixture 961_stmt_temp_owned_call (copyAtDefault and plain `ret T` as arguments leak 0 buffers, was 200 per 200 temporaries; an alias-returning callee leaves the list intact). Full suite 613/0. VERSION 0.1.117.

- [x] #14060407 {difficulty:4} [compiler/runtime — Math.sqrt and friends are calls into the runtime object] docs/float4-design.md §6.4: Math.sqrt lowers to rae_ext_Math_sqrt, an extern defined in the separately compiled runtime, so every scalar square root in hot code (the physics solver's friction and rolling clamps, vector lengths) is a real call that cannot inline. Make the pure scalar math externs (sqrt, and whichever of floor/ceil/abs/min/max/sin/cos are runtime calls) inline intrinsics in the generated C (static inline in rae_runtime.h, or direct libm/builtin calls), keeping the bits identical (sqrtf is IEEE); check fixtures 948-959 stay bit-exact and measure benchmarks/float4_solver. — DONE: sqrt, floor, ceil, round, remainder and floatBits/floatFromBits are static inline in rae_runtime.h (out of runtime_buffers_math.c); the generated prototype after them is compatible C, so nothing in the emitter changed. abs/min/max were already Rae functions. The transcendental ones (sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 pow exp log) stay out of line on purpose: libm does not round them correctly, so a C compiler folding sinf(constant) with its own implementation (GCC/MPFR) could change the bits. Verified: the release rae_scalar binary has no sqrt call (3 fsqrt); fixtures 948-959 bit-exact at default and (948, 958) release profile; benchmarks/float4_solver rae_scalar 603.6 -> 588.1 ms (load ~4, indicative), all five checksums still match; noted in docs/float4-design.md §6.4. Deviations from §0, recorded in docs/float4-design.md §0.1: and/or/not/any are keywords so the mask functions are both/either/invert/anyLane/allLanes; Mask4 lanes are UInt32 fields (no private fields in Rae); mulAdd(a,b,c) = a*b + c; with two or more NaN inputs the result is a quiet NaN equal to one of them (the C compiler may commute a scalar x + y, which the fixture caught); added negate, embedIndex (the other half of minLaneIndex) and lowering(). - [x] #95614691 {difficulty:4} [compiler: value binding from a view-returning call emits invalid C] `let transform: Transform3D = componentView(this: transforms, entityId: entityId)` (componentView returns `view T`) passes sema but generates C that assigns a `const rae_Transform3D*` to a `rae_Transform3D`, which clang rejects. The language already had the rule: a value binding may not take a call that returns a reference, and the diagnostic says to bind the view first ('let source: view T => ...'), then copy. The check read the call's resolved declaration, which a generic call does not have yet in sema (the backend specializes it), so componentView and any generic `ret view T` slipped through to invalid C. sema_call_returns_reference (sema.c) now answers for an unresolved generic call from the program's functions of that name: a reference when every candidate returns one. - [x] #19451472 {difficulty:4} [compiler — `ret componentView(...)` from a function that returns a value type emits the reference: gcc fails] In a function declared `ret Transform3D`, `ret componentView(this: table, entityId: id)` (componentView returns `view T`) passes sema, and the C backend emits `rae_Transform3D __ret_val = <const rae_Transform3D*>` ("initializing 'rae_Transform3D' with an expression of incompatible type 'const rae_Transform3D *'"). Found in lib/physicsScenes/port/VehicleSpawn.rae chassisTransform, worked around with componentCopy. Either copy out of the view on return (view T returned as T copies, like a `let x: T = viewExpr`) or reject it in sema with a clear message; add a fixture. — Done (2026-10-05). Chose the reject option, since the language already rejects the `let` form: spec 2.3.1 refuses `let t: T = <reference-returning call>` with "copying what it refers to must be spelled out", and a value `ret` is the same implicit copy. Copying on `ret` would have made `ret` quietly do what `let` refuses. Sema's ret case (compiler/src/sema.c) now raises "this call returns a reference, and this function returns a value; ... bind it first ('let source: view T => ...'), then 'ret source'" for a plain, a generic or a componentView call and for an `opt T` return; forwarding with `ret view` stays legal. Both forms failed in gcc before. Spec 2.3.1 gained the ret paragraph. Fixtures: 1003_reject_ret_reference_call_as_value (the four rejected forms, forwarding legal) and 1004_ret_copy_from_named_view (the spelled-out repair runs; a String-carrying struct is deep-copied and independent; nothing outstanding at exit). All 80 active examples still pass sema+emit. Full suite 655/0. Version 0.1.163.

Moving a List FIELD with `own` zeroes the source (the C does copy + memset), but moving an `opt` field does not: `holder.second = own holder.first` (both `opt List(Int)`) emits `__asg = holder.first; drop(&holder.second); holder.second = __asg;`, so `holder.first` still owns the buffer, and a following `holder.first = none` (or holder's own drop) frees what `holder.second` now holds. Repro: type Holder { first: opt List(Int) second: opt List(Int) }; var holder: Holder = { first: items, second: none }; holder.second = own holder.first; holder.first = none; then read holder.second (reads freed memory; in the renderer it aborted with 'pointer being freed was not allocated'). Make `own` of an opt (or any owning) field empty its source like the List case, and add a fixture that checks it under RAE_MEM_STATS (and ASan if the runner has it). — Done: c_expr.c's AST_EXPR_OWN emptying move excluded opt places (`!ptr->is_opt`); a zeroed opt is none, so the same copy + memset now covers them. Repro: a Main.rae with `import Math` and that line; `rae run --target compiled`. When the scale is at minScale and frames still miss, it sets capFps = 30; to restore 60 it needs 180 consecutive frames with dt <= overBudgetSec (1.25/60 = 20.8 ms), but while capped capFrameSleep pads every frame to 33 ms, so every capped frame counts as missed and goodFrames never reaches 180: an app that dipped once stays at 30 fps until restarted (seen on an iPhone 15 Pro: 59, then 55 as the scale stepped down, then 30 for good). Fix: judge a frame by its WORK time (start of frame to just before the cap's padding sleep), not by the padded dt — e.g. capFrameSleep records the frame's work seconds on the controller and updateRenderScale uses them while capped. Also: the thermal 'critical' state forces capFps 30, and lifting it should depend on the thermal state falling again, not only on frame times. Test first (a compiler test case or lib test): a controller driven to the cap by missed frames, then fed 180+ frames whose work time is 10 ms but whose dt is 33 ms (padded), must restore capFps 60; a controller fed genuinely slow work must stay capped. Keep the existing behavior otherwise (drop after 4 misses, 30-frame cooldown, restore one rung after ~3 s good). EXAMPLES: verify on 114_walker_character (the only example with the dynamic-resolution controller): force misses until it caps at 30 (e.g. a heavy setting or a slowed GPU), then let it run light and see the cap lift (log render.capFps). A fixed-width integer reference is a plain pointer (no `rae_View_*` wrapper), and the narrowed binding's uses skip the deref the wrapped types get. Passing an `opt Int` local or `none` works; a binding does wrap (`let x: opt Int = 4`). Wrap a non-optional argument into the parameter's optional (`(rae_opt_T){ .has = 1, .value = ... }`) for every value-optional parameter mode (`opt copy` / `opt own`) and payload (numbers, fixed-width ints, Bool, String, structs), and add a fixture passing a literal, a local, a field and a call result.

A bare literal correctly takes its context's type (binding, argument, arithmetic operand — Rust/Swift/Go/Zig/C# do the same), but one that does not FIT that type must be a sema error naming the value, the type and its range ("300 does not fit UInt8 (0 to 255)"), never a silent wrap. - [x] #75768925 {difficulty:4} [language — a numeric literal cast to the type it already gets is an error; sweep the tree] Depends on the literal range-check task above. A bare literal already takes its context's type in Rae (`var frameEnd: UInt64 = 0`, `takesWide(count: 0)`, `bytes.add(value: 0)` on a List(UInt8) all work), so `0 as UInt64` there is noise — 257 `<number> as <IntType/FloatType>` spellings in lib/, examples/, benchmarks/ and compiler/tests (e.g. lib/gpu/FramePacer.rae `var frameEnd: UInt64 = 0 as UInt64`). Decision 2026-10-13: make it a sema ERROR, not a warning (same one-spelling principle as `-1` over `0 - 1`; warnings pile up): when a numeric literal is cast with `as T` and T is exactly the type the literal would take from its context, reject it with "the literal already is a T here; drop `as T`". A cast that converts (`count as Float`), or a literal cast where no context gives it a type, stays legal. Land the rule and the sweep in ONE commit (breaking: bump PATCH): remove every redundant cast the new error reports, keep the ones it does not, and check the generated C is unchanged where it should be (emit-c every example, the benchmarks compile check, the full suite). Add the rule to AGENTS.md (Coding style: next to the `-1` rule) and spec/rae.md (literals). Fixtures: one rejecting the redundant forms (binding, argument, List element, arithmetic operand), one accepting the converting and context-free forms.

- [x] #16483925 [compiler bug: `copy` and `own` parameters are read-only in the function body] `func f(a: copy Particle) { a.x = 7 }` fails with "cannot mutate through read-only view 'a'", and `a = { x: 8, name: "c" }` with "cannot assign to read-only view identifier 'a'"; `own` is the same (probed 2026-10-20 in /tmp/bindprobe r7_copy / r7_own). A `copy` or `own` parameter is the callee's own value, like a `var`: its fields and the whole value must be writable, and writing it never reaches the caller (the caller's value stays as it was for `copy`; for `own` the caller's name has ended). Find where sema marks these parameters read-only (the view check is applied to them), fix it, and add a case: write a field and the whole value of a `copy` and an `own` parameter, and check the caller's `let` value is unchanged after the `copy` call. Only `view` parameters stay read-only. — DONE: sema.c (function parameters into the symbol table) took every struct parameter that was not `mod` or `view` as a view parameter (read-only), which caught `copy` and `own` too. Now only `view` is read-only (a bare struct parameter, already an error, stays read-only so it gives one error, not two). The generated C already gave the callee its own deep copy, so writes never reach the caller. New case 1166_copy_own_params_writable: fields (including a List field) and the whole value of a `copy` and an `own` parameter written; the caller's `let` unchanged after the copy calls; no leaks at exit. - [x] #88140274 [binding `=` 1/6: the semantics doc] Decision 2026-10-20: `=` is the only binder; `=>` goes. A binding's mode on the same line decides what the name denotes: no mode = a fresh deep copy of the right-hand side; `view T` / `mod T` = an alias of the place on the right; `own x` on the right = a move. Replace (not patch) the old README argument ('`=` always copies, `=>` always aliases, so the operator carries the meaning') with: '`=` initializes a binding of the declared type; `view T` and `mod T` are types whose values are aliases, exactly as they already are for parameters and `loop let`. Aliasing is marked by the mode keyword everywhere, and nowhere else.' State the one subtlety: `=` on a declaration line initializes; `=` on any other line writes into the place the name denotes; aliases can never be rebound (so `let m: mod Particle = world.a` then `m = world.b` deep-copies world.b INTO world.a, it is not a rebind), and a `view` on the left of a non-declaration `=` is an error. Write the approved table into docs/binding-modes-design.md (the 2026-09-30 option N section) and the README binding section, rows: (1) `let x: T = v`: not rebindable, no `x = v`, no `x.f = v`; (2) `var x: T = v`: `x = v` replaces x with a deep copy, fields writable, the source never changes; (3) `let x: view T = place`: no rebind, no write, no field write (errors 'cannot assign through read-only view' / 'cannot mutate through read-only view'); (4) `let x: mod T = place`: no rebind, `x = v` deep-copies v into the place, fields writable; (5) `var x: view T` / `var x: mod T`: errors ('aliases are bind-once; declare with let'); (6) `loop let x: view T in list` read-only, `loop let x: mod T in list` writes the element (`x = v` deep-copies into it), `loop var x: mod T` an error, `loop var x: T` a writable local copy; (7) parameters: bare `a: T` an error, `view` read-only, `mod` writes the caller's place (`a = v` deep-copies into it) and a `let` cannot be passed to it. Errors in every alias row: a view/mod of a temporary (`let v: view T = makeThing()`: 'cannot bind a reference to a call that returns ownership'), a `view` passed on to `mod`, and (from step 2) a `mod` alias or `mod` loop over a `let`. Record that `var x: mod T` was considered and rejected: `var` means rebindable and aliases never are. Docs only, one commit. — DONE: docs/binding-modes-design.md §1 now opens with the 2026-10-20 decision (the three meanings, the step-1 sentence, the one subtlety with the `m = world.b` write-through example, the approved 7-row table with its error messages, the errors shared by every alias row, and `var x: mod T` recorded as rejected); its examples, the matrix header and §3's refactoring bullet use `=`, and the status line says the compiler keeps `=>` until the parser step. README.md: the '`=` copies, `=>` binds' bullet and the 'operator carries the meaning' argument are replaced by the new sentence, a 'Bindings, one table' section holds the table, and its code examples use `=` (they compile once step 3 lands; examples/09_playlist, which the first one mirrors, is swept in step 4). Docs only; no code or tests changed.

Make all three the ambiguity error consts already give, naming both modules and the fix (qualify it, or open only one). Overloads inside ONE module (same name, other labels) stay legal. Keep what works: with the lib module only imported, the bare name is the project's and `Module.name` the lib's, and a lib's own code keeps its own names (case 1168). New cases for (1)-(3). - [x] #14407207 {difficulty:4} Compiler bug: type and enum names must belong to their module, like every other name. Today they are program-wide: two modules that both declare `type Point` cannot be in one program at all (sema.c sema_report_duplicate_type, case 989 'type names are program-wide'), even when the program only IMPORTS one of them (probe: `import Device` plus a project `type Pointer { x: Int }` is refused because lib/Device has `enum Pointer`). So a lib adding a type can break any program that has one of the same name, though nothing there opens it. Rae's module rule already says how it should work: a type is reached bare in its own module and the modules the file opens, and as `Module.Type` through import; two opened modules with the same type name make a bare use ambiguous at the USE, not an error at the declaration. Make the compiler do that: type identity is module plus name in the type registry, C names carry the module (so two `Point` structs both emit), generics, component tables, reflection and the JSON/state formats keep working (a type's written name stays its own name). Case 989 changes to two `Point` types living side by side, each module using its own, plus cases for `Module.Type` through import, the ambiguity at a bare use with both opened, and a lib type next to a same-named project type under import. Large: split if needed (registry and C names first, then the use-site rules). Build every example and run the suite. VISUAL TESTS OK. — DONE (compiler 0.2.101), in one step (no split needed): the type registry already keyed a struct by its declaration, so the work was the NAMES. New src/type_names.c runs at the start of sema over the merged program: for a type/enum name declared in two files or more, every declaration but one gets an internal name carrying its module (`Point__in_points_Right`; a lib declaration keeps the written name, so a type the compiler knows by name keeps it; an internal name cannot be written, a type name has no `_`), and every use — type refs, literals, casts, generic args, `X.case`, `X.create`, match patterns — is pointed at the declaration its file sees: its own file's, else the one visible bare (an explicit open picks between two project modules), else the one it imports. Two visible bare is an error at the USE: 'type 'Pointer' is ambiguous: it is declared in both 'Device' and 'input/Pointers', which are both open here; open only one of them'. The same pass resolves the new `Module.Type` (parser: a qualifier on a type ref; formatter prints it) in types and expressions (`Device.Pointer.fine`), through import/open/`as`, and errors on a type the module does not have. type_written_name gives the written name back for string conversion, typeName (fields loops, generic params) and so JSON/component names. One module declaring a type twice is still an error ('declared twice in one module'). Cases: 989 is now 989_same_type_name_two_modules (two Points side by side: literals, List(Point), toJson/fromJson), 1189 (import Device + a project Pointer: bare is the project's, Device.Pointer the lib's), 1190 (ambiguous bare use with both open, and an unknown Device.Nothing), 1191 (declared twice in one module). Also checked by hand: two modules' generic Box(T) and enum Kind (match, is, toString), ComponentTable(Point) + typeName, no leaks. Screenshots of 143 looking across the forest; PC frame time; the phone setting with fewer views. — Done: app3d/FarCanopy + lib/CanopyBake (+canopy_bake.wgsl): every non-empty 40 m PropField cell is one cluster impostor (829 clusters of all 31090 trees in 143), baked at load in one GPU submission (66 ms) from the trees' own impostors (a quad per tree, its view nearest the cluster view, baked depth), drawn by the sprite pass's impostor mode (3 views blended, lit through the G-buffer, quad depth) out to 1800 m. Atlas pages share layers (subjectsPerSide, past the 256-layer limit); clusters are framed to their box per view (impostorExtents) in 128x32 cells so wide low clusters fill their side views. Hand-over 270-330 m: a cell's trees fade out as its cluster fades in, both from the cluster center with its seed; far trees now stop at 370 m unthinned (they were thinned and drawn up to 2x). PC 3x3 views ~330 MB; phone setting (RAE_SIMULATE_MOBILE=1) 2x2 views of 64x16, nearest only, ~36 MB, 27 ms. PC frame time: walking view unchanged (10.0 ms), 28 m-up view 10.4 -> 10.9 ms. Screenshots noon/dusk/phone in looks-development rendering/treeLod/6-*; checks/impostorBake bakes a 4-cell canopy and checks its mips; the 143 gate checks every tree is in a cluster; full suite passes.
- [x] #67582117 [tree LOD follow-up: the far canopy loses trees] lib/app3d/FarCanopy / lib/CanopyBake. In a downstream game's sparse hill forest (about 3,000 trees of 14 kinds over a 1 km hill, the PropField's cells 32 m, the canopy from 450 m with a 60 m band; built exactly as WalkerTerrain does: planFarCanopy on the farSpritesOf list, bakeFarCanopy from the trees' impostor atlas with defaultCanopySettings, 474 clusters, 8 layers) the clusters seen from 700-800 m show far fewer trees than the same trees as single FarSprites impostors to 2 km: the flat umbrella pines and the palms are nearly gone (a few pixels or nothing), the spruces and cypresses come through thinned. 143 from 1.1 km looks dense but mostly yellow crowns, so it may lose its darker or flatter species too. Find where (the cluster view framing of a wide low box in a 128 x 32 cell, the trees' quad size from the tree atlas's frame, the coverage of thin crowns in the cluster mips) and make a cluster show what its trees show at that distance. Test: a cluster of one species at a time compared with its trees as FarSprites at the same distance (covered pixels within a few percent), for every GroveTrees species; before/after screenshots of 143 from a fixed RAE_CAMERA_AT at 1 km. — Done: new checks/canopyCoverage renders one 40 m cell of each species as a cluster and as its trees with the sprite pass shader (150/700/1100 m, four directions between views); clusters kept 0-77% of their trees. Fixed five causes: (1) canopy_bake read the tree frames 2 vec4 apart after the box framing made them 3 (most species baked with another's frame or not at all); (2) filtered edge reads mixed empty texels' depth 0 (far back) in: depth and thickness now stored times coverage, divided by the filtered alpha; (3) a 40 m deep cluster seen between views 45 degrees apart: box framed atlases now march each view along the fragment's own ray (impostorMarch, per-texel thickness from the tree's mirrored front; normal stored octahedral to make room), PC canopy 4x4 views of 96x24 (same memory), phone 3x3 of 48x12; (4) one view marched per fragment, picked by weight with a dither; (5) a cluster's quad now stands at its box's front, so slopes no longer hide its front trees. Clusters now keep 88-104% (phone 91-120%). Cost about 1.5 ms in views across the forest (10.3->11.6 ms from 28 m up, 9.3->11.0 ms from 1.1 km; walking view unchanged) after front-to-back order, step count from texels crossed (max 12) and a coarse empty-ray skip. Screenshots from RAE_CAMERA_AT '1 0.0 0.3 -0.02 8.0 0.0 -1100.0 40.0 0.0 0.0 0 0' in looks-development rendering/treeLod/7-*: the 1 km band shows every species (spruces, cypresses, reds) where it was mostly yellow crowns. Gates, 11 checks and the full suite pass.
- [x] #75215750 Far canopy cost: the per-pixel march of app3d/FarCanopy clusters (sprite_billboard.wgsl impostorMarch) costs about 1.5 ms on PC in views across 143's forest (from 28 m up or 1.1 km away), mostly empty fragments of clusters overlapping low across the forest. Already done: front-to-back order, steps from texels crossed (max 12), a coarse empty-ray skip. Try a tighter per-view outline than the box, a coarser level for far clusters, or culling clusters fully hidden behind nearer ones; checks/canopyCoverage must stay within its tolerance. — Done: new bench mode RAE_CANOPY_BENCH=1 in checks/canopyCoverage times a 1.2 km forest of 900 clusters on the GPU (marched vs not; steady where app frame times swing). It showed the 5 halvings after each candidate were half the march. Now a step already in the prop is a hit without halving, else 3 halvings with an allowance for the depth the remaining interval spans; the ray's atlas point and depth are worked out once (linear in t). Bench: 3.1 -> 2.0 ms (500 m outside the forest) and 1.9 -> 1.3 ms (28 m up), unmarched 0.4/0.3; coverage unchanged (89-103% PC, phone cypress better, 105-112%). In 143 the two views across the forest are back at their unmarched frame times (about 9.2 and 10.3 ms). Tried and dropped (measured): a coarser level for far clusters (cost is in the near ones; blurs there), narrowing the march with coarse reads (forest clusters rarely empty at that level), 10 steps (7%, less coverage); a tighter outline or hidden-cluster culling would only save the empty fragments, which the coarse skip already makes cheap (0.4 ms for all of them). 1 km band picture unchanged. 143/137 gates, checks and full suite pass.
- [x] #34023913 Compiler bug: a second `let` of the same name in one function body passes the checker and only clang stops it ("redefinition of 'straight' with a different type" in the emitted C). Found in a test file that had `let straight: List(Vec3) = ...` and later `let straight: Aim = ...` (a struct) in the same `main`. The checker should refuse the second binding (or the language say it shadows) with an error naming both lines. Fixture: the two lets, rejected by the checker. — Done: sema_check_rebinding (compiler/src/sema.c) refuses a let/var/const whose name is already bound in the same scope, naming the first line ("'straight' is already bound on line 19 in the same scope ... rename one of them"), and a parameter's name at the top of a function body (that also reached clang). An `if let` binding now has its own checker scope, matching the C block the backend gives it: before, the name stayed visible to the checker after the statement, so two `if let x` in a row (common in lib/, e.g. `if let made`) would have collided. A nested block may still shadow (it already worked; now pinned by a case). Also refused: a loop's own variable redefined at the top of its body (C would allow it; nothing in the tree does it). Fixtures 1229_let_same_name_twice (the task's List then struct pair, same type twice, a parameter, a loop variable: all rejected) and 1230_let_shadows_in_nested_block (nested shadowing and repeated if-let names run). Full suite passes; all 89 examples and checks emit cleanly. docs/binding-modes-design.md §1 notes the rule; VERSION 0.2.112.

SUMU (the SUMU repo, AGENTS.md "Boundaries") makes sdk/ and every app separate packages so the compiler enforces that an app uses only the SDK and the SDK never reaches the Shell or an app; this leak lets that rule break silently. Add fixtures for both directions (dependent without import: error, already true; dependency calling its dependent: error, new), and the same for two sibling dependencies (one must not see the other unless it depends on it). DONE: the compiler holds package boundaries when a project has dependencies: a dependency never reaches the project above it (a bare call, a qualified call or a type is "unknown ... here: it is declared in the project that depends on package 'sdk'" in the dependency's file); a dependency reaches another only if its OWN pack declares it (each dependency's .raepack is read as a library pack, targets optional, and its dependencies resolved); the project scan skips dependency folders inside the tree, so a dependency is reached only by `import x/...`. sema_package_reaches gates bare calls, qualified calls and type names (rae_deps_owner_of / rae_deps_package_reaches). Cases 1276 (reach up: error), 1277 (dependent without import: error), 1278 (undeclared sibling: error), 1279 (dependency of a dependency: runs). QUEUE_BACKLOG #131 closed. Full suite 929/929. A pure-Rae protocol layer with no I/O (functions over bytes and time, so it is tested without a network), in lib/net: a connection handshake with a timeout, sequence numbers and acks in every packet header, a reliable ordered channel (resend on missing ack, with a round-trip estimate), an unreliable sequenced channel (old packets dropped), fragmenting and joining a message bigger than one packet (packets kept under 1200 bytes), keep-alive and disconnect. Own Rae code, not a wrapped C library (runtime C rule). Fixtures drive two endpoints by hand: every reliable message arrives once and in order under loss, unreliable ones never arrive out of order, a fragmented message survives a lost fragment, a silent peer times out. Zero allocations per packet after warmup. Done: lib/net/Connection.rae (handshake, acks, keep-alive, timeouts, disconnect, unreliable sequenced channel), lib/net/ReliableChannel.rae (send/receive windows, fragments), lib/net/Wire.rae (bytes, wrapping sequences); fixture 1263_connection_protocol. - [x] #80949146 Compiler bug (silent wrong code): inside a generic function, a call to an overloaded user function whose argument has the type parameter's type always picks the FIRST overload, for every instantiation. Repro: `func encode(value: view Position, ...)` and `func encode(value: view Health, ...)`, then `func encodeOne(T: type, value: view T, ...) { encode(value: value, ...) }` called with Position and with Health: both run the Position version (direct calls pick correctly). Either resolve per instantiation or reject the call; add a fixture. lib/net/replication avoids it by using field reflection. Done: the C backend's own callee choice (c_call.c emit_call_expr, c_discovery.c) took the first same-name, same-arity candidate; inside a specialized generic body the call arrives unlinked, so every instantiation ran the first overload. It now prefers the non-generic overload whose parameter types are the arguments' concrete types, and an overload set that takes none of a struct argument's type is a compile error. Fixtures 1273_generic_overload_per_instantiation, 1274_generic_overload_no_match.

Also, in an earlier form of compiler/tests/cases/1272_replication, `let seat: Seat = game.seats.copyAtFallback(index: 0, fallback: spare)` (a List field of a local struct, a named fallback) kept ~340 buffers per call while the same copy from a local List kept none; not reduced yet. It is now `fallback: copy T`, as Array's already was: a temporary is freed in range, a named one is copied and the copy freed, and an out-of-range result no longer shares its buffer with the caller's variable (found while fixing). The 1272 seat case: 335 buffers left at exit with bare T, 0 with copy T. Fixture 1275_copy_at_fallback_owns_fallback.

PROPOSAL, to check and improve: (1) the pin is committed in the project; (2) one shared store of built toolchains per commit, with its own clone, so projects on one commit share one build and nothing appears as a worktree here; (3) the tool lives in Rae, not in each project: `rae toolchain pin <commit>`, `rae toolchain update` (moves to the latest main only if the project still builds), `rae toolchain gc` (removes pins nothing uses); (4) an explicit override for working on Rae and a project together, RAE_ROOT=<checkout> for one command; (5) a normal build does not change the pin, only the pin commands do, which today's rae.lock does not separate; (6) the iOS frameworks and the SQLite build are shared the same way. THE PACKAGE MANAGER IS PART OF THIS, and the user wants these questions answered in a decision record before building, and to be asked where the answer is theirs. The user's current thinking: a package manager has to be built into the Rae compiler, OR be a separate tool written in Rae that the compiler uses and that users never see. If the package manager needs deep compiler syntax knowledge, it may be better inside the compiler, because that skips the bootstrapping issues. The questions: (a) inside the compiler, or a separate tool written in Rae that the compiler calls invisibly? (b) How much does it really need from the compiler's parser and semantics: only reading .raepack and rae.lock, or also imports and module resolution? (c) If it is written in Rae, what builds it on a fresh machine, which Rae version builds it when the project is pinned to another one, and how is it shipped? (d) Are the toolchain and the package manager one system, with one lockfile, one store and one resolver, since rae.lock already holds both a toolchain line and dep lines? (e) What should happen to what already exists: the compiler already has `rae add`, `fetch`, `update` and `tree`, path and git dependencies cloned into .rae/deps/<name>, and `dependencies` in .raepack, with a registry deliberately out of scope (docs/raepack-v2-and-packages.md section 15). Extend that, or replace it? (f) Is a registry still out of scope once there are several projects to share packages between? Do not run the migration before the decision record is agreed. — DECIDED, not built: docs/toolchain-and-packages-decision.md is agreed: a generated ./rae per project instead of PATH; the manager in the C compiler; the .raepack as the one file; a required exact version with an optional commit, no ranges; several packages per repo; no registry; the stdlib stays one version for now. Seen in examples/146_treeLab createLab (LabState, built in an `unsafe` block and returned; worked around by assigning those fields after the literal); a small program with the same default did not reproduce it, so the trigger also needs the function-level pool mark that createLab has. - [postponed] #15828977 [sound: a real-time audio engine, design first] Rae has no audio/sound at all. Decide if we use the term sound or audio for the feature. I assume audio as we will have video later. Explore and design, before any code, an audio layer good enough for a real-time DAW and synthesizer and a video editor, on macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS and Android (and the web where it can): low-latency output and input (a callback on a real-time thread with no allocation or locks in it, the buffer size and sample rate the device gives, glitch-free under load), a mixer graph (tracks, buses, gain, pan, sends, effects), sample-accurate timing and scheduling (a sound or a note at an exact sample, a clock shared with video), streaming decode of long files (MP3, AAC, Ogg, FLAC, WAV; licences per AGENTS.md, and check the rules for doing our own in Rae vs using existing library, and what is the language of that library. Possibly abstracting via a Rae audio API is an option too.) next to short sounds held in memory, MIDI in and out, resampling, and each platform's backend (Core Audio / AVAudioEngine, WASAPI, ALSA / PipeWire / PulseAudio, AAudio / Oboe, Web Audio) with the host's audio session rules (iOS: the session category, ducking or mixing with other apps' sound, playing through the ring/silent switch, interruptions by a call, route changes such as headphones). Read how proven engines are built (miniaudio, JUCE, PortAudio, CLAP and VST3 hosts, Ardour, Bitwig's and Ableton's public talks) and write docs/sound-design.md: the layers, the real-time thread rules, the APIs a program sees, what lands first, and how it is tested headless (an offline render compared with a reference). No ad hoc sound before the design. NOTE: SUMU needs it too, from the first step that plays sound: short sounds for alarms (a task's time, a timer's end; mixed with music, ducking it, and heard with the phone on silent but not during Do Not Disturb or a Focus), and later a proper music player (MP3 files, play and pause, seek, a queue, playing on with the app in the background and the lock screen's controls). SUMU will later also speak (text to speech) through it. — DONE: the design is docs/audio-design.md (the term is "audio"; the file is named for it). The six build steps of its §11 are queued below as "[audio 1/6] … [audio 6/6]"; its §13 lists the open decisions (D1 vendored miniaudio + decoders, D2 calling Rae from C, D3 marking real-time functions, D4 Atomic(T), D5 program node kinds, D6 lib/audio vs a package, D7 SUMU alarm vs Focus, D8 ASIO/PipeWire/Oboe).

Now the locals are saved into their frame slots first and the arguments are packed from those slots (twin_args_from_frame, as a child call does), so the extern writes the slot and the restore reads it. Checked every blocking extern: only Sys.rae_sys_read_file_bytes (outLen) and Image.nativeLoadPng (width, height; it already worked, its mod arguments point at the caller's storage) take mod. The graph types moved to wait_graph.h and --report-waits to may_wait_report.c (may_wait.c was at 993 lines). lib/ promises marked (math, clock, buf_zero, rae_str_len, atomics, Signal.post/tryWait, signal wait noAlloc, SpscRing push/pop/count, the Realtime calls). Full suite 1101 passed. QUESTION: Which way? A) make every overlap an error and rewrite the 46 call sites (read the part into a local first, or pass narrower parts); or B) make mod+mod an error (4 sites) and let the compiler pass an overlapping view argument as a copy taken at the call (no source changes for the other 42+2; a copy at those calls, deep for a list or large struct); or C) neither for now (keep the warning mode, no restrict). After A or B I build the rule, flip stress 13 to handles, then restrict on List data pointers in counted loops, measured. — ANSWERED 2026-11-12: no rule for now (option C): a whole and its part, even both as mod, is a legitimate pattern (fields never move); no exclusive-access rule, stress 13 stays as the record of the behavior, the warning mode stays off by default. Recorded in docs/realtime-language-design.md §4.6 "Decided" and §9 R8. The restrict step moves to "[realtime 6a2: measure DSP vectorization, then restrict proved per function]", which builds it only if it pays and without any rule.

- [x] #72033795 [lib/net: a reliable message of several fragments stalls the channel under duplicates] Found by the media editor's session server (mediaeditor packages/session, tests/session; it now sends its snapshots in parts of one fragment to stay clear of it). Between two lib/net Connections (default config) through lib/net/BadNetwork with loss 12, latency 40, jitter 20, reorder 8 (hold 30) and duplicate 3: one reliable message of 6000 bytes (6 fragments) then 100 messages of 4 bytes, all handed to the channel. With seeds 2, 5 and 7 of 1..8 the receiver gets 59 of the 101 and never more (the sender ends with nothing in flight: it saw every fragment acked), so 42 are lost while the sender thinks them delivered; with a first message of 4 bytes, or with no reorder/duplicate, all 101 arrive every time. 59 = 1 + 58, about one window (64) of fragments, so a duplicated or late fragment of the multi-fragment message probably lands in a reused slot after the window wraps (ReliableChannel's receiver taking an old id as a new one, or an ack of a stale slot). Fix it and add a fixture: the run above with seeds 1..20 delivers all 101 in order every time, sender and receiver agreeing; and the same with messages of 2 to 64 fragments mixed with small ones. Done 2026-11-17: the cause was the ack, not the slots: the sender's window starts at its oldest unacked fragment, the receiver's at the first fragment of the oldest message it has not delivered (it waits for the whole message, and for the app to take it), so with a message of several fragments the sender sent ids past the receiver's window; the receiver refused them but the packet was still acked, so the sender saw them delivered (in the reported run ids 64 and 65 came while message 0's fragments were still incomplete). The same lost messages with single-fragment ones when the app takes its messages late. Now a packet carrying a fragment ahead of the receive window (ReliableChannel.reliableIsAhead) is not acked (Connection notes its sequence only after reading its messages) and the fragment comes again. Rae 0.4.10. Checked: case 1530_reliable_fragments_duplicates (BadNetwork loss 12, latency 40, jitter 20, reorder 8 held 30, duplicate 3; every message checked whole and in order, the sender with nothing in flight): the reported run 20 of 20 seeds, messages of 2..64 fragments with small ones 20 of 20, 300 small messages taken every 500 ms 20 of 20; on the unfixed library the same case gives 10, 2 and 0 of 20; the 37 net cases pass.

Breaking changes are allowed, and the way UI layers are rendered may change fundamentally; it must still use the ECS model for UI. WHY: today there are two separate orders and they do not meet. (1) Inside the scene UI, ui/Layer's LayerRoot stack (content 0, dock 100, back-button 200, dialog 300, debug 400) and raised nodes (raiseNodeToLayer, used by app3d/ModeMenu's "..." menu). (2) Between whole blocks, ui/HudOverlay's HudOverlay entities (world labels 10, the whole scene UI 20, log strip 80, debug readout 90, OverlayDraw.app for an app's own). The whole scene UI, with its dialog layer, is ONE overlay; so anything an app paints directly on the Gpu2dCanvas (a compass, a kill feed, health bars, a reticle, a full-screen map, a QR code over a button) is either under every scene node or over every scene node, dialogs included. The game had its feed and compass over the open "..." menu and over its Map/Look buttons (an iPhone screenshot); it now draws them under the scene UI with an app overlay at order 15, which works only because nothing of its own must go above some scene nodes and under others (its full-screen map and a QR code painted over a button still cannot). webgpu-2d-ui-renderer.md §5 says painter's order today): (a) ONE ordered stack of named layers for everything drawn in 2D: scene nodes, world labels (3D-anchored text and bars), an app's immediate canvas drawing, the log strip, debug readouts; an app or a system draws into a layer by name (or a layer entity) and gets the order right without knowing the others; (b) standard layers an app gets by default, in this order at least: world-anchored (names, bars over 3D), HUD, HUD over (e.g. a full-screen map), dock/toolbars, popovers, dialogs and context menus (modal), toasts/notifications that must stay under a modal dialog, debug; an app adds its own between them; (c) z order inside a layer that does not depend only on tree order or mount order, and nodes raised out of their parent's subtree (as raiseNodeToLayer) keeping their layout and clip rules clear; (d) INPUT in the same order as paint: hit tests top layer first; a modal dialog or an open context menu takes every press, tap and drag under it (touch sticks, the camera's touch turn, buttons), and a tap outside closes it; immediate-drawn things can register hit areas in their layer; (e) transparency and effects: alpha blending in order, a layer's opacity, a dim or a blur behind a dialog (ui/BackdropComponents), shadows, clipping and safe areas per layer; (f) animation (docs/ui-animation-design.md): a layer's or a node's opacity, offset and scale animated, dialogs and toasts sliding in, without breaking the order; (g) layout stays independent of paint order (ui-coordinate-and-responsive-layout.md, the safe area); (h) performance: few draw calls and batches across layers (the instanced quads and SDF text of webgpu-2d-ui-renderer.md), no per-frame allocation, the scene UI's culling and dirty tracking kept, cost measured on a phone; (i) developer experience: a .raescene says a node's layer and z, the scene editor (example 121) shows and edits them, ui/HudOverlay and ui/Layer become one concept or one clearly built on the other, a debug view lists what is drawn in which layer; (j) the 3D walker apps (app3d/HudOverlays, ModeMenu, SettingsDialog, the touch stick) and the examples moved to it, with tests: unit tests of the order and of input under a modal, and a frame where an app's canvas drawing sits between two scene layers.
